llm.reply:
Marfan syndrome is a well-characterized connective tissue disorder [1] with a range of documented ocular, skeletal, and cardiovascular phenotypic features recorded in its MedGen record [2].

## Clinical Features

MedGen lists these clinical features: Aortic regurgitation [7], Arachnodactyly [11], Astigmatism [15], Ectopia lentis [19] and Esotropia [23]. It also lists Exotropia [25], Pes planus [26], Glaucoma [27], Congestive heart failure [28], Hypertropia [29] and Micrognathia [30].

## Genetic and Systemic Basis

The condition is a multisystem connective tissue disease inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and mainly caused by mutation of the FBN1 gene, producing variable clinical manifestations [22: "multisystem connective tissue disease with autosomal dominant inheritance"][22: "mainly caused by FBN1 gene mutation and often has different clinical manifestations"].

## Diagnosis and Care

Diagnosis relies on the Ghent II Nosology criteria to identify patients at high risk for complications, and management emphasizes screening, assessment, and ongoing follow-up [24: "The Ghent II Nosology of MFS criteria are crucial in MFS diagnosis, guiding clinicians in identifying high-risk patients"][24: "importance of screenings, assessments, and close follow-ups to optimize the continuum of care"].

MedGen's record for Marfan syndrome lists a broad set of clinical features spanning cardiovascular, ocular, and skeletal systems [2]. MedGen lists these clinical features: Aortic regurgitation [7], Arachnodactyly [11], Astigmatism [15], Ectopia lentis [19], Esotropia [23], Exotropia [25], Pes planus [26], Glaucoma [27], Congestive heart failure [28], Hypertropia [29] and Micrognathia [30].

## Disease Identity And Records

The condition is identified in publications and databases simply as Marfan syndrome [1][14][18], and also appears in a literature entity record as Marfan Syndrome [3]. A related PubMed entry directly poses and answers the question What Is Marfan Syndrome? [10]

## Underlying Biology And Course

Marfan syndrome is described as a multisystem connective tissue disease with autosomal dominant inheritance that is mainly caused by FBN1 gene mutation and often has different clinical manifestations, with a neonatal form that is especially rare, severe, and carries a poor prognosis [22: "Marfan syndrome (MFS) is a multisystem connective tissue disease with autosomal dominant inheritance"][22: "Neonatal MFS is especially rare with severe conditions and a poor prognosis"]. A comprehensive review covers the condition's epidemiology, etiology, clinical presentations, diagnostics, complications, and treatment modalities, noting that the Ghent II Nosology criteria are used to guide identification of high-risk patients [24: "covering its epidemiology, etiology, clinical presentations, diagnostics, complications, and treatment modalities"][24: "The Ghent II Nosology of MFS criteria are crucial in MFS diagnosis, guiding clinicians in identifying high-risk patients"]. A separate review states that there is still no radical treatment method for the condition, though early identification, diagnosis, and treatment can effectively prolong patients' life span [22: "there is still no radical treatment method for MFS, but early identification, early diagnosis, and early treatment can effectively prolong the life span of patients"].

## Related Publications And Trials

Further literature on the condition includes a review titled [Latest advances in the diagnosis and treatment of Marfan syndrome] [6], along with publications indexed under PubMed identifiers pmid=2402263 [5], pmid=35894201 [9], pmid=37058316 [13], pmid=38517496 [17], and pmid=8733052 [21]. Associated clinical trials include one named Studies of Heritable Disorders of Connective Tissue [4], one named Comparison of Two Medications Aimed at Slowing Aortic Root Enlargement in Individuals With Marfan Syndrome [8], one named Angiotensin Converting Enzyme Inhibitors in Marfan Syndrome [12], one named Losartan Versus Atenolol for the Treatment of Marfan Syndrome [16], and one named A Randomized, Open-label, LOSARTAN Therapy on the Progression of Aortic Root Dilation in Patients With Marfan Syndrome [20].
